← Freelance retainer calculator

How many hours should a freelance retainer include?

The useful answer is not a universal number. It is the largest package you can deliver this month without giving one client most of your capacity.

Start from capacity, not from what the client asked for

A 20-hour retainer is cheap to promise and expensive to keep if only 65% of your calendar is billable. If you have 160 available hours and 65% utilization, you have 104 billable hours — not 160. The retainer has to fit inside that 104, after admin, other clients, and recovery.

Leave a buffer you can name

Revisions, Slack questions, and “quick looks” are the work that makes a vague retainer unprofitable. Put a scope buffer in the price and write included hours, response time, and out-of-scope rates into the agreement. Unlimited access is not a package size.

Do not sell more than half the month to one client

If one retainer uses more than 50% of billable capacity, a late invoice or a paused project becomes a cash-flow event. Quote a range — 10, 15, 20 hours — and let the client buy the size that fits both of you.

Same income goal, five package sizes

On the calculator’s default plan ($6,000 take-home, $1,800 costs, 160 hours, 65% utilization, 15% buffer) the hourly floor is $75 and a 20-hour retainer prices at $1,725. The table uses that same floor; only included hours change.

How many hours should a freelance retainer include?

Include a scope you can finish inside realistic billable hours, keep a revision buffer, and avoid committing more than half of your billable month to one client. Compare 10, 15, 20, 25, and 30 hour packages against the same income goal before you send a number.

Why isn't 20 hours the right default for every retainer?

Twenty hours is cheap to promise and expensive to keep if only 65% of your calendar is billable. On a 160-hour month at 65% utilization you have 104 billable hours, not 160. The package has to fit inside that 104 after other clients and recovery.

Why this is different from a basic hourly-rate calculator

A $75 rate means little if only 65% of your month is billable, your tools and taxes cost $1,800, and a vague retainer absorbs unplanned revisions. This calculator makes each assumption visible so you can change it before making a promise.

Common question: this clears my floor — so why am I still short?

Because the floor rate is your revenue target divided by your whole billable capacity: it is the rate that works if every one of those hours sells. On the default plan the $1,725 retainer clears a $75/hr floor and is still only 22% of a $7,800 target — the rest rides on 84 hours nobody has bought yet, at a fill rate of 96.4%. Enter what you already have committed and the share of the rest you honestly expect to bill, and the goal check above prices that assumption instead of hiding it. Why clearing your floor is not reaching your goal works through the numbers.

Common question: how many hours should a retainer include?

Start with a scope you can deliver inside your billable capacity, then leave the buffer intact. A retainer is a commitment of access and work, not permission for unlimited requests. Compare 10, 15, 20, 25, and 30 hour packages on this page, or read the longer answer in how many hours a retainer should include. Put included hours, response time, and out-of-scope pricing in your agreement.

Common question: should I sell a retainer or stay hourly?

Price the block first, then look at real usage. If they typically use half the hours, the retainer collects unused-hour cash — and often does not renew. If they can blow past the included hours without billed overage, your effective rate falls below the floor. Retainer vs hourly at real usage walks through the default numbers.

Common question: should unused hours roll over?

A leftover hour that rolls into next month is work you deliver without a second invoice. On the default 20-hour block, a 10-hour first month plus unlimited rollover into a full second month is 30 hours for $1,725 — $57.50/hr, $750 below the floor. Cap rollover at the 3-hour buffer and month 2 stays at $75/hr. See expire vs cap vs unlimited rollover.

Common question: should I accept Net 30?

A monthly price is not cash in the bank. Invoicing at month-end plus Net 30 means about 60 days before the first payment. If you cannot float that month of take-home and costs from savings or other clients, ask for prepaid. See how payment terms change the cash you float.

Common question: should I use this or a paid tool like Bonsai?

Different jobs. Bonsai is a paid subscription for running a freelance business end to end — proposals, contracts, invoicing, and time tracking. This calculator answers the narrower question that comes first: what the retainer price should actually be, checked against your hourly floor. See this calculator vs. Bonsai.

Common question: should I use this or a paid tool like Harvest?

Different jobs. Harvest is a paid subscription for logging billable hours and invoicing for them after the work starts. This calculator answers the question that comes before any of that: what the retainer price should actually be, checked against your hourly floor. See this calculator vs. Harvest.

Common question: why not just divide my income goal by my hours?

That division skips two numbers this calculator adds: monthly business costs and a scope buffer. On the default plan it prices a 20-hour retainer at $1,153.85; this calculator, adding $1,800 in costs and a 15% buffer, prices the same block at $1,725.00 — $571.15 a month left uncovered by the income-only guess. See this calculator vs. pricing from income alone.

Common questions

Should I charge a monthly retainer or bill hourly?

A retainer usually pays you more when the client uses less than the included hours, and less when they use more than the break-even hours without billed overage. This calculator prices the retainer from your capacity, then shows both sides at 50%, 75%, 100%, and 125% of the block.

When does a retainer drop below my hourly rate?

Divide the monthly retainer by your hourly floor. That is the unpaid-overage break-even. On the default plan a $1,725 / 20-hour retainer covers a $75 floor up to 23 hours; a 25-hour month with no overage lands at $69/hr.

How many hours should a monthly retainer include?

Include only hours you can deliver inside your billable capacity, and avoid selling more than half of that capacity to one client. Compare 10, 15, 20, 25, and 30 hour packages against the same income goal so you can quote a range instead of one number.

Should unused retainer hours roll over?

Only if the rolled hours still leave month 2 at or above your hourly floor. On the default $1,725 / 20-hour plan, a 10-hour first month plus unlimited rollover into a full second month is 30 hours for $1,725 — $57.50/hr, $750 of unpaid time. Cap rollover at the 3-hour buffer and month 2 stays at $75/hr.

Should I accept Net 30 on a freelance retainer?

Only if you can float the monthly revenue target for the days until first cash. Invoicing at month-end plus Net 30 is about 60 days. If you cannot float that amount from savings or other clients, require prepaid or 50% on kickoff.

retainer-payment-terms.html.text:
← Freelance retainer calculator

A retainer price is not cash in the bank.

Freelancers often accept Net 30 on a monthly retainer, then work 30–60 days before the first payment lands. The cash you must float is a pricing decision, not a courtesy.

Your monthly revenue target

Take-home plus business costs and taxes. The default $7,800 is the calculator’s default plan.

CASH YOU LEND THE CLIENT

Days until first cash × monthly target ÷ 30. Arithmetic only.
If they pay Days Cash to float

How the float is calculated

Take the monthly revenue target — take-home plus business costs and taxes — and multiply by days until first cash divided by 30. That is the savings or other-client cash you need while this retainer is unpaid.

  • Prepaid on kickoff: 0 days, no float.
  • Invoice on kickoff, Net 15: about 15 days, half a month.
  • Invoice on kickoff, Net 30: about 30 days, one month.
  • Invoice at month-end, Net 15: about 45 days.
  • Invoice at month-end, Net 30: about 60 days, two months.

If a $7,800 monthly target is billed at month-end plus Net 30, you float $15,600 before first cash. That is not a late fee. It is working capital you are lending the client.

What to put in the agreement

Write the payment trigger, not just “Net 30”. Prepaid on kickoff, or invoice on the first of each month due on receipt, removes the silent extra month. 50% on kickoff and 50% on the invoice date splits the float if the client will not prepay in full.

Price the block first, then check the float. Open the retainer calculator to pair this with usage. Retainer vs hourly is the one-month failure mode. Unused-hour rollover is the two-month version of the same gift.

This page is a planning aid, not financial or legal advice. Review the numbers and the contract before you send either. Hosted URLs, when they exist, carry no availability SLA.

Common questions

Should I accept Net 30 on a freelance retainer?

Only if you can float one monthly revenue target for the days until first cash. Month-end invoicing plus Net 30 is about 60 days. If you cannot float that amount, require prepaid or 50% on kickoff.

How much cash do I need to float a retainer?

Multiply the monthly take-home plus costs by days-until-cash divided by 30. Prepaid is zero. Kickoff plus Net 30 is one month. Month-end plus Net 30 is two months.

retainer-vs-hourly.html.text:
← Freelance retainer calculator

Retainer vs hourly: unused hours pay you; unpaid extras do not.

Freelancers search this because a 20-hour block looks clean on a proposal and messy three months later. The question is not “is a retainer better.” It is “better at what usage.”

On the calculator’s default plan — $6,000 take-home, $1,800 costs, 160 available hours, 65% utilization, 20 included hours, 15% buffer — the floor is $75/hr and the retainer is $1,725. Full use is $86.25/hr. That is the buffer working.

Same $1,725 retainer against the $75 floor at four usage levels. Arithmetic only.

100% of the block20 h$1,725$1,500$86.25Yes
125% of the block25 h$1,725$1,875$69.00No

The unpaid-overage break-even is $1,725 ÷ $75 = 23 hours. Past that, every extra hour without a billed overage line is a gift. Bill those 5 extra hours at the floor and 25 hours still pays $84/hr — the buffer, restored.

The 10-hour month is the other failure mode. You collected $975 more than hourly. The client paid for access they did not use. That is the usual reason a light-use retainer does not renew. Shorten the block or stay hourly if that is the real pattern.

Open the calculator, enter your own income goal and included hours, and read the table before you send the proposal. After the price looks right, check whether unused hours that roll over still cover the floor, then check whether Net 30 still leaves you able to float first cash. Nothing is uploaded.

This page is arithmetic, not financial or legal advice. It does not tell you to accept, reject, or rewrite a contract. Hosted URLs, when they exist, carry no availability SLA.

Common questions

Is a retainer better than hourly for a freelancer?

It depends on how many hours the client actually uses. A retainer pays you more when usage is light and less when they exceed the unpaid break-even without billed overage. On a $1,725 / 20-hour block with a $75 floor, 10 hours of use is $172.50/hr for you and 25 hours with no overage is $69/hr.

How do I know when a retainer stops covering my hourly rate?

Divide the monthly price by your hourly floor. That many hours is the unpaid-overage break-even. Put billed overage at the floor rate in the agreement so months above that number still cover.

unused-hour-rollover.html.text:
← Freelance retainer calculator

Unused hours that roll over are unpaid work next month.

Clients ask for rollover because a quiet first month feels like they overpaid. The clause they want is a second month where you deliver the leftover for free. Price that gift before you write it.

The quoted block

Defaults match the calculator’s $1,725 / 20-hour plan at a $75 floor. Month 1 at 50% leaves 10 hours. Month 2 uses the full new block plus whatever rolled.

UNPAID HOURS NEXT MONTH

Unused after month 10 hours
Month 2 if leftover rolls0 hours
Expire vs cap-at-buffer vs unlimited one-month rollover. Arithmetic only.
If the agreement says Hours rolled Month 2 hours Month 2 $/hr Covers floor? Unpaid gift

How the gift is calculated

Month 1 unused hours = included hours minus hours they actually used. Month 2 hours under unlimited rollover = new-block hours plus that leftover. Month 2 effective rate = monthly price ÷ those hours. The unpaid gift is leftover hours × hourly floor.

  • Default $1,725 / 20 hours / $75 floor.
  • Month 1 at 50%: 10 hours used, 10 leftover.
  • Expire: month 2 is 20 hours at $86.25/hr. Gift $0.
  • Cap at the 3-hour buffer: month 2 is 23 hours at $75/hr. Gift $225.
  • Unlimited rollover: month 2 is 30 hours at $57.50/hr. Gift $750.

The 3-hour buffer is the unpaid-overage break-even minus included hours ($1,725 ÷ $75 − 20). A cap there keeps a catch-up month on the floor. Unlimited rollover spends that buffer and then some.

What to put in the agreement

Write “unused hours expire at month-end” or “up to N unused hours may roll once, then expire or bill at the floor.” Do not write “hours roll over” with no cap and no expiry. A quiet first month plus a catch-up second month is the usual pattern after a kickoff delay, a vacation, or a stakeholder who was not ready.

Price the block first, then check rollover, then check the float. Open the retainer calculator to pair this with usage. Retainer vs hourly is the one-month view. Payment terms is the cash-float view.

This page is a planning aid, not financial or legal advice. Review the numbers and the contract before you send either. Hosted URLs, when they exist, carry no availability SLA.

Common questions

Should unused retainer hours roll over?

Only if the rolled hours still leave month 2 at or above your hourly floor. On the default $1,725 / 20-hour plan, a 10-hour first month plus unlimited rollover into a full second month is 30 hours for $1,725 — $57.50/hr, $750 of unpaid time. Cap rollover at the 3-hour buffer and month 2 stays at $75/hr.

How do I cap unused-hour rollover without killing the deal?

Cap rolled hours at the unpaid-overage buffer — monthly price divided by hourly floor, minus included hours. On the default plan that is 3 hours. Hours above the cap expire or bill at the floor.

vs-bonsai.html.text:
← Freelance retainer calculator

This calculator vs. Bonsai

Different jobs: one prices a retainer, the other runs the paperwork around a freelance business.

Bonsai is a well-known paid subscription platform for freelancers, built to run the business side of the work — proposals, contracts, invoicing, and time tracking, described on hellobonsai.com. Its templates include a retainer agreement, and it publishes a general hourly-rate explorer by skill and role. It is the kind of tool a freelancer reaches for once they already have a price and need the paperwork and billing built around it.

That is a different job from the one this page does. This calculator has no invoicing, no contracts, no client records, and no account. It exists for the narrower task that comes before any of that: turning your income goal, real billable capacity, operating costs, and scope buffer into a defensible retainer price — and checking that price still covers your hourly floor at light use, full use, and overage, with nothing to sign up for.

What each tool answers.
QuestionWhere to answer it
What should I charge for this retainer, given my costs, capacity, and income goal? This calculator — it prices the block from your own numbers and checks the price against your hourly floor at 50%, 75%, 100%, and 125% usage.
How do I send the client a proposal, contract, and recurring invoice for that price? Bonsai or a comparable paid platform — proposal drafting, e-signatures, and billing are jobs this page does not attempt.
Does an unused-hour rollover clause or Net 30 still leave me able to float the month? This calculator — the rollover and payment-terms pages model exactly that, with no account and nothing uploaded.
Do I need time tracking, client CRM, or a shared workspace across several ongoing clients? Bonsai or a comparable paid platform — this page remembers nothing about your clients between visits except what your own browser stores locally.

This calculator is deliberately the opposite shape from a subscription platform: nothing to sign up for, nothing billed monthly, and nothing typed here ever leaves your browser. That makes it useful for pricing one retainer honestly before you open any proposal tool — and the wrong tool for running the invoicing, contracts, and client records of an ongoing freelance business, which is exactly the job a paid platform like Bonsai is built for.

It needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or a paid tool like Bonsai?

They answer different questions. Bonsai is a paid subscription platform for running a freelance business end to end — invoicing, contracts, proposals, and time tracking, with a retainer agreement template among its documents, described on its own site. This calculator does none of that. It answers one narrower question first: from your income goal, real billable capacity, costs, and a scope buffer, what should the retainer price actually be, and does it still cover your hourly floor at light, full, and heavy usage. Once you have that number, Bonsai (or any contract tool) is where you might draft the agreement around it.

This calculator vs. Harvest

Different jobs: one prices a retainer before the work starts, the other tracks and invoices the hours after it does.

Harvest is a well-known paid time-tracking and invoicing subscription, described on getharvest.com. It logs billable hours with start/stop timers, manual entries, idle-time detection, and offline tracking; records expenses with attached receipts; generates invoices that pull in the logged time and billable expenses automatically, with online payment through Stripe or PayPal; and reports on billable hours, utilization, and project profitability. It is the kind of tool a freelancer reaches for once a retainer is already priced and the work has started, to track the hours against it and bill for them.

vs-pricing-from-income-goal-alone.html.text:
← Freelance retainer calculator

This calculator vs. pricing from your income goal alone

The fastest way to price a retainer is take-home income divided by billable hours. This page is about what changes when business costs and a scope buffer are added to that division instead of left out.

Pricing from income alone means taking the monthly take-home a freelancer wants, dividing it by the hours they expect to bill, and quoting a retainer off that single number — nothing added for software, insurance, self-employment tax, or the revisions a real engagement tends to produce. It is one division, it takes no time, and because dividing two numbers always produces an answer, the result looks like a real rate even though half of what it needs to cover was never in the calculation.

This calculator takes the same income goal and adds the two figures that method skips: monthly business costs and a scope buffer for the extras a client relationship generates. It runs once, in the browser, on nothing that leaves the device, and it prices the retainer from what actually has to be covered rather than from take-home pay by itself.

The gap is not rounding error. On this calculator's own shipped example — a $6,000 income goal, 160 available hours, 65% utilization, $1,800 in monthly business costs, a 20-hour retainer, and a 15% scope buffer — dividing income alone by billable capacity (6,000 ÷ 104 billable hours × 20 hours) prices the retainer at $1,153.85. This calculator, folding in the $1,800 of costs and the 15% buffer, prices the same 20-hour block at $1,725.00. That is $571.15 a month — $6,853.80 a year — that the income-only guess quietly treats as free: money spent running the business, or hours spent on scope drift, delivered to the client at no charge.

Two ways to answer "what should the retainer be".
QuestionWhere to answer it
I want a number in ten seconds and I have not looked at my business costs. Income divided by billable hours — free, but blind to costs and scope drift.
What should this retainer actually cost, once my costs and a buffer are counted? This calculator — free, instant, private, no account, no upload.
Is a rate built on income alone actually covering what the business spends? Run the same numbers through this calculator and compare the two prices directly.
Does this retainer still clear my income goal once the rest of the month is priced in honestly? This calculator's income-goal check, not a single division.
Do I need to create an account, upload financial data, or sign up? No, for either approach — the division needs nothing and neither does this calculator.

The income-only division is not a bad habit so much as a shortcut whose cost stays invisible until a slow month or an unusually demanding client makes it obvious. This calculator keeps the shortcut's convenience — still one page, still free, still nothing to sign into — it just adds the two numbers that were missing from the division.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Why not just divide my income goal by my billable hours?

Because a retainer priced that way only ever covers take-home pay. Software, insurance, a laptop replacement fund, and self-employment tax do not stop needing money because a client pays on time, and none of that is in an income goal by itself. A scope buffer is missing too: a retainer without one prices the hours a client is expected to use, not the revisions and small extras that actually show up. Skip both and the number still looks like a real rate, because dividing two numbers always produces one -- it is just the wrong one.

How much difference does it actually make?

On this calculator's own shipped example -- a $6,000 income goal, 160 available hours, 65% utilization, $1,800 in monthly business costs, a 20-hour retainer, and a 15% scope buffer -- dividing income alone by billable capacity prices the retainer at $1,153.85. This calculator, adding the $1,800 in costs and the 15% buffer, prices the same retainer at $1,725.00. That is $571.15 a month, or $6,853.80 a year, quietly absorbed as an unpaid business expense instead of billed to the client who is using the hours.

Where would the extra costs come from?

From whatever it costs to run the practice for a month: software subscriptions, business insurance, a coworking desk or home-office share, an accountant, marketing, hardware replacement set aside monthly, and the self-employment tax portion an employee's paycheck would have withheld automatically. None of that has to be exact to be worth entering -- a rough monthly total from a bank statement is already closer to the truth than leaving the field at zero, which is what pricing from income alone does by omission.

What if I don't have a scope buffer figured out yet?

A buffer between 10% and 20% is a reasonable default until a freelancer has enough retainer months behind them to know their own pattern of small unplanned requests. The buffer is not padding for its own sake -- it is priced-in room for the revision or two that almost every ongoing engagement produces, so that a normal month does not quietly run over the hours a client bought.

Is this the same as looking at last year's tax return?

No, and it does not replace a tax return, a bookkeeper, or an accountant. Those confirm what already happened and what is owed. This calculator does the one thing neither hands over on its own: turning an income goal, real billable capacity, monthly costs, and a scope buffer into a single retainer price, before the work starts. It is arithmetic on numbers a freelancer supplies, not a tax or accounting determination.

Open the retainer calculator to price your own plan, then check it against the income-goal check.

will-this-retainer-hit-my-income-goal.ht.text:
← Freelance retainer calculator

Your floor rate assumes the whole month sells. It usually doesn’t.

Every “what should I charge” calculator divides your income goal by your billable hours. That answer is only true at a fill rate almost nobody hits — and the number it hides is bigger than the one it shows.

The arithmetic that goes missing

Take the calculator’s default plan: $6,000 take-home, $1,800 of costs and taxes, 160 available hours, 65% realistic utilization, a 20-hour retainer, 15% scope buffer.

That gives 104 billable hours against a $7,800 monthly revenue target, so the hourly floor is $75 and the retainer prices at $1,725. Send it and the tool is right: the client clears your floor, with buffer to spare.

But $1,725 is 22% of $7,800. The other $6,075 has to come out of the 84 hours you have not sold to anyone. Nothing in the floor rate says so — the division that produced it already assumed those hours were sold.

What that assumption costs at real fill rates

The same $1,725 retainer, the same $75 floor, against a $7,800 target. Only the share of the 84 unsold hours you actually bill changes. Arithmetic only.
You bill this share of unsold hours Hours billed Month reaches Short of goal Hours that would close it
100%84.0 h$8,025None — $225 over—
80%67.2 h$6,765$1,03513.8 h
60%50.4 h$5,505$2,29530.6 h
40%33.6 h$4,245$3,55547.4 h

The break-even is the useful number: this plan needs a 96.4% fill rate on its unsold hours before the goal arrives. Not 96% utilization — utilization is already priced in, at 65%. Ninety-six percent of the hours left after that haircut, sold and billed, every month.

That is the bet a $1,725 quote is making. It may be a fine bet. It should not be an invisible one.

Two ways to close the gap, and how to tell which is smaller

At a 60% fill rate the plan is $2,295 short. That is either:

  • 30.6 more billed hours — a 96.4% fill rate instead of 60%, from this client, another client, or better sales; or
  • a retainer priced at $4,020 instead of $1,725, closing the gap without selling one extra hour.

Usually the answer is neither on its own: a second retainer at half the gap and a modest price rise. Entering the other client’s revenue and hours into the calculator shows what is left to find after both.

And when the required fill rate comes back above 100%, that is a different answer, not a harder version of the same one. It means billing every hour you have still misses the goal. Selling cannot fix it; the price, the capacity, or the take-home number has to move.

Why the tool doesn’t just lower your floor

It would be easy to divide by expected-fill hours instead and print a bigger floor rate. That produces a rate you cannot quote — one that prices your scarcity into every hour and loses the work. The gap is real, but the fix is usually a different client mix rather than a number the market will not pay. So the calculator keeps the floor honest and reports the gap separately, where you can act on it.

Open the calculator, fill in your income goal, then add what you already have committed and the share of remaining hours you honestly expect to bill. Once the month adds up, check the price against real usage, check what rollover costs you, and check how much cash Net 30 makes you float. Everything runs in your browser; nothing is uploaded.

This page is arithmetic, not financial, tax, or legal advice. It does not tell you what to charge or which clients to take. Hosted URLs, when they exist, carry no availability SLA.

Common questions

Why does my freelance rate calculator say I am fine when I am not making my income goal?

Most rate calculators divide your monthly revenue target by your billable capacity. That gives the rate that works only if every billable hour in the month gets sold. A single retainer can clear that rate exactly and still be a small fraction of the month. On a $7,800 target with 104 billable hours, a 20-hour retainer at $1,725 is 22% of the target; the other 78% depends on filling 84 hours you have not sold yet.

What fill rate does my retainer price assume?

Divide the revenue you still need after the retainer by your unsold hours times your floor rate. On the default plan that is $6,075 ÷ (84 hours × $75) = 96%. If you do not bill 96% of your non-retainer capacity, the price does not reach the goal, however well it clears the floor.

Should I raise my retainer price or find more clients?

Both close the same gap and the arithmetic tells you which is smaller. At a realistic 60% fill rate the default plan is $2,295 short, which is either 30.6 more billed hours or a retainer priced at $4,020 instead of $1,725. If the required fill rate is above 100%, selling cannot close it at all and the price, the capacity, or the goal has to change.
